texto: this film fails on every single level. it immediately begins with its corny, over the top message right in your face dialogue. i accept it. maybe it's because it's translated from German. seriously, it's very obvious this was written for people who are not very smart. i don't care about a single character sincerely. they all seem like empty dolls to die. why should i care if they do, honestly. i hated paul so much when he died i started clapping, because i was going to be actually mad if they didn't kill him. not because war is hell or whatever but because he's so unlikeable and dumb and boring. he's the placeholder for a human but this isn't a video game. why do i care about anything this stupid, boring, annoying man goes through. i don't. all of the cinematography was a blatant ripoff of 1917. not a single element of the original (1930) film is to be seen here. the most memorable parts of that movie aren't even Frankenstein'd into this mess they're just forgotten. the hands on the barbed wire. them in the trenches for days at a time, shaking in the overwhelming noise of the constant bombing and shelling. the crosses going over the young boys who we learned to know and watched march to their deaths. nothing here is memorable or even likeable. there are stupid horns that sound like dubstep sometimes and it honestly feels disrespectful to the actual victims. I've never once hated a soundtrack so much to feel like it was disrespectful to real life, but this feels like it is. all of the characters lack basic common sense and don't even act like human beings. i don't think any of them are even trying to survive (understandable). daniel bruhl pisses on his shoe at one point. a dude stabs himself to death with a fork. there is no humanity to be found here. the ending marches the soldiers to their deaths post cease fire just in case you didn't understand war is meaningless. the main character stands up and dies awkwardly in what is supposed to be a cinematic shot or whatever and then a boy takes his dog tags like he did at the start. subtlety is dead. i guess they thought perhaps we were too stupid to understand basic metaphors, human dialogue or anything that isn't shoved down our throats. the scene that left the biggest mark on me from the first film was when a soldier steals his dead friend's boots, simply because he needs them to continue on. it made me weep. the scene which is arguably the climax of the film were the main character kills a French soldier in a trench and then regrets it is so overdone and bland here that i didn't even cry (i easily cry at any and all films). this film tortures you so much all i felt was tired, but it still didn't convince me war is hell. i can see it now, a little boy who was swayed by internet opinions and happens to idolize the Germans actions watching this and still thinking it was worth it, and that the main character died fighting with honor. it fails at every single possible thing. the beginning is supposed to be school boys naively joining the army and then showing us the reality of the brutality of war but this film is so eager to start it even butchers that by giving us a beginning sequence which screams the messaging in your face before the actual film has even started. they could've just left that as a short film and left me alone. this was a completely useless jerkoff fest made by people who can't understand the themes of a very simple book. there is a complete lack of empathy for any of the soldiers in this film which is hilarious because that's seemingly the entire point of it (for you to empathize with the German soldiers who died for an evil and wrong cause). i do have plenty of empathy for the fact that these were just people but somehow the film is simultaneously too nice to them and too uncaring at the same time. it doesn't understand its own message and neither do i. the only part of this film i enjoyed is the trench sequence right next to when the French's tanks showed up and a little after that, i enjoyed around 30 minutes of this film. the rest of it is a complete mess.

I had read some of the notoriously negative German reviews of this when it released with a few calling it war kitsch and one review even saying it's retroactively a right wing film in how it leans into the stab in the back theory that was so popular amongst post WW1 right wingers. Needless to say my expectations where low and in the intervening time I'd read the book which I had enjoyed. I was utterly shocked with how dull and flatly shite this film is. It's main fault is a vague timbre of genericism that pervades every part of it, non descript music, flat acting, dull pacing and many war tropes combine to create a totally banal experience. The only point I really liked was the opening sequence where a dead soldiers tunic is scavenged, repaired and handed to Paul, our protagonist. The film however goes downhill from here, it removes the crucial section from the 1930 film and book where Paul returns home and meets his ever jingoistic teacher and adds in a truly useless subplot following a German politician negotiating the armistice and a grim general desperate to fight to the bitter end. Both storylines take up crucial time from Paul and his comrades, time which in the wonderful 1930 film added levity and camaraderie, a thing that barely exists here. In fact in some ways this film is orgisatically obsessed with grimness and violence,.it does so with the same shlocky gore that Hacksaw Ridge revelled in, another shite war film. It would be forgivable I'd the battle sequences where well done but they have rigid and unrealistic quality to them that detracts from their effect, the French use flamethrowers at point blank range whereas in reality they would have been used at a further distance, tanks fight without infantry support. This is coupled with the disjointed nature of the film due to the added storylines and the setting around the last week for the war the film tries to add a Dunkirk/Nolanesque countdown clockwork mechanism that is just daft and a far cry from the leviathan feeling of the book and original film where time moves over the course of years as Paul grows rougher, more weary. Here we have a rushed opening sequence after which most of the movie takes place around the last week with Paul being stabbed by a Frenchman at 11 o'clock as the war ends. It's so crazy and dumb in fact that after the soldier pulls the bayonet from Paul's body and the blood pours out we hear another Frenchman outside say, "It's 11, stop fighting!" FUCK OFF LIKE. That is something a child writes and this movie won four Oscars. The book and original film rather end with Paul being banally shot by a rogue sniper with the backdrop of an otherwise quiet frontline. I think it is obvious which is more effective. The real sadness of this film is all the people that will watch it and revel in it and enjoy it and will never watch the original and actually experience just how good that film is and how superior it is. A totally dull affair and not worth any time

Nouvelle adaptation du roman d’Erich Maria Remarque, le film d’Edward Berger entend faire éprouver physiquement l’horreur de 14-18. Tranchées, boue, mutilations, agonies, rats, chevaux morts : rien n’est épargné au spectateur, tandis que le contraste avec le confort des états-majors souligne l’inhumanité du massacre. La démonstration est techniquement impressionnante, mais son insistance finit par en révéler la limite. À force de mouvements de caméra étudiés, de raccords spectaculaires et de compositions soigneusement travaillées, Berger esthétise précisément la violence qu’il prétend dénoncer. Cette fascination formelle introduit une certaine complaisance dans un propos antimilitariste par ailleurs fort peu neuf : un siècle après les faits, fallait-il encore deux heures trente pour nous apprendre que la Grande Guerre fut une boucherie ? L’ampleur de la production impressionne davantage que son regard. Un film de guerre puissant dans sa fabrication, mais dont le spectaculaire finit paradoxalement par affaiblir la dénonciation.

Impressive movie, but they absolutely miss the key themes of the book and turn the plot into what it wasn’t meant to be, a showing of the epic huge loud battles and brutality. The clue is in the name here, this movie misses the mark. The biggest betrayal is the omission of the key scenes of Paul returning home, and how he is treated by those around him versus who he has become and how he feels. The focus is put on parts of the war that, although essential, are not the focus of the book, which is what makes the book so special in the first place! I’m sure if I’d seen the movie first I’m sure I would have enjoyed it much more. My first dislike is the focus on the idea of them being young boys and inexperienced. In the book, there is no confusion that the boys are young, but by this point they were the older group, and this is again so important to the book. To make them young and inexperienced is to take away the fact that they are young and yet they have so much experience and are numb to everything now. My other problem is the omission entirely of the Catholic hospital recovery scenes. I understand that you must omit things, and so normally I wouldn’t have a problem with the omission of such a scene for times sake. But they omitted these scenes so they could focus on the war and battle aspect of the movies, which again IS NOT MEANT TO BE THE FOCUS. The changing of the scene with the French soldier makes no sense to me, while of course still emotionally devastating, to begin the scene with Paul moving across the crater to stab the man I feel removes the desperation element of the act, and makes the remorse feel less genuine. Furthermore, they change not only Paul’s ending, instead of dying on a normal day he dies minutes before the armistice in an epic battle. I can’t understand why they did this (well I can, blockbuster drama) but I really hate it, the way he dies is meaningful and integral to the feeling you get after finishing the book. Finally, they include armistice discussions which are not at all mentioned in the book. This is just a mind boggling decision, as again I might remind you, the name suggests the book is about the everyday life on the front NOT ABOUT THE WAR ITSELF. There are enough movies about the politicians who ended the war, but the reason, again, that this book is so important is that this is emitted. Those on the front had no idea these talks were going on, had no idea what tomorrow would bring let alone and were forgotten and abandoned by those in power, purely cannon fodder to continue and unnecessary and futile war. Basically, if you want a good movie about life as a German soldier in World War I watch this movie, but you like the book, do not watch this movie. It cuts out important parts of the book that make it a masterpiece  in favour of nothing special. I was honestly pretty confused about what was going on at times and it lacked a certain flow to the plot. The movie also completely misses the mark in terms of the book. Rather than portraying an emotional struggle, the movie portrayed a sort of physical brutality present in war, but lacked any philosophical thought the book offers. Additionally, the plot was very different from the book’s and they made many very unnecessary changes. I also think it also fell short in the task to portray a friendship between the soldiers and the main character, which was a guiding and reoccurring theme in the book. I simply wasn’t very impressed with the movie and while it did invoke sympathy (as it should when one sees many 18 yr olds stabbed and blown to shreds), it didn’t offer anything past that. I wasn’t eager to continue watching or even to finish the movie. The only good thing it offered was its cinematography, which alone cannot make up for anything that it lacks. The book was far better and I don’t understand why everyone is so impressed with this shitshow of a movie.

I appreciated what the film was trying to do more than I appreciated watching it. War movies usually have one of two failure modes. The first is accidentally making war look exciting. The second is spending three hours insisting that war is bad, as though the audience arrived expecting a TED Talk titled “Actually, trench warfare seems underrated.” All Quiet on the Western Front mostly avoids the first trap, then walks straight into the second. Every scene is calibrated toward the same conclusion: young men are chewed up by institutions that barely notice their existence. This is true. It is also established about thirty minutes in. The remaining two hours mostly increase the fidelity of the suffering rather than the depth of the argument. The craftsmanship is undeniable. The cinematography is gorgeous in a way that feels almost inappropriate. The sound design is relentless. The performances are excellent. But I kept waiting for the movie to tell me something about the psychology of war, nationalism, courage, fear, or even ordinary survival that I didn’t already know. Instead, it kept turning the volume up on a point it had already made. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe war really is just endless repetition punctuated by arbitrary death. But a movie isn’t obligated to reproduce the experience of its subject. Sometimes it should interpret it. Beautifully made, emotionally exhausting, and ultimately less interesting than the history that inspired it.

“One day we received orders to storm a French position. We got in, and my comrades fell at the right and left of me. I was soon confronted by a French corporal—he with his bayonet at the ready and me with my bayonet at the ready. For a moment, I felt the fear of death. And in a fraction of a second, I realized that he was after my life exactly like I was after his. I was quicker than he was. I tossed his rifle away, and I ran my bayonet through his chest. He fell, put his hand on the place where I had hit him, and then I thrust again. Blood came out of his mouth, and he died. I felt physically ill, and I nearly vomited. My knees shook, and I was, frankly, quite ashamed of myself. My comrades were absolutely undisturbed by what had happened. One had boasted that he killed a Frenchman with the butt of his rifle. Another had strangled a French captain. A third had hit another over the head with his spade. And they were all ordinary men like me. One of them a train conductor. Another, a commercial traveler. Two were students. The rest were farm workers. Ordinary people that never would’ve thought to do any harm to anyone. How did it come about—that we could be so cruel? We were told that a good soldier kills without thinking of their adversary as a human being. The moment a soldier sees in his adversary a fellow man, he’s not a good soldier anymore. But I had in front of me the dead French soldier. And oh, how would I have liked him to raise his hand. I would’ve shaken it, and we would’ve been the best of friends. He was like me, but a poor boy armed with the most cruel weapons against a man whom I had nothing against personally. He only wore the uniform of another nation who spoke another language, but a man, who had a father and mother and a family perhaps. I woke at night, sometimes drenched in sweat because I saw the eyes of my fallen adversary. And I tried to convince myself what would’ve happened to me if I hadn’t been quicker than he. What would’ve happened to me if I hadn’t first thrust my bayonet into his belly? What was it that we soldiers stabbed each other, strangled each other, went for each other like mad dogs? What was it that we who had nothing against them personally, fought with them to the very end in death? We were civilized people after all, but I felt that either side’s culture is but a very thin lacquer which chips off the very moment it comes into contact with cruel things like real war. To fire at each other from a distance—to drop bombs—is something impersonal. But to see each other in the whites of the eyes and then to run with a bayonet against a man—it was against my conception and against my inner feeling.” Stefan Westmann German Army Corporal (WWI) 29th Infantry Division

Le plan d'ouverture, puis de fin, est peut-être l’une des plus belles manières d’exposer la futilité de la guerre dans un seul dialogue, juste un simple plan fixe sur une forêt. Néanmoins, le film prend le parti de suivre les négociations de l’armistice en parallèle de l’histoire des protagonistes. Or, dans le livre, c’est justement l’absence totale de point de vue autre que celui de Paul qui rend le récit si tragique. À chaque instant, la guerre pourrait s’arrêter dans 2 minutes ou dans 10 ans, ça ne fait aucune différence pour les soldats engagés. Pire, le film introduit à la moitié cet espèce de compte à rebours avant l’armistice pour rajouter de la tension, décision qui dessert totalement son propos. Autre parti pris décevant, l’incarnation d’un grand méchant par le général allemand. “Regardez comme c’est dommage, tout les gens aux autres postes de commandement étaient bien intentionnés, c’est juste un seul méchant monsieur qui cause la mort de tout ces jeunes”. Encore une fois, dans le livre, personne n’est nommé comme responsable de la souffrance des soldats. Toute l’horreur repose là-dedans : des gamins de 20 ans, pris dans un engrenage bien au-delà de leur échelle, et aussi inutile qu’implacable. Une réalité beaucoup plus nuancée et dure que le sosie de Dr Eggman qu’on retrouve. En bref, un film qui incarne visuellement très bien les horreurs de la guerre, mais qui omet totalement les éléments narratifs les plus essentiels du matériel de base. O cineasta François Truffaut possui uma frase popular: “não existe filme antiguerra”. Em sua tese ele conceitua e discorre sobre a linguagem sensual e entretida do cinema, isso leva a conclusão que não importa o quanto você faça um filme sobre guerra, mostrando inúmeros lados horríveis deste acontecimento horrível, o cinema sempre vai romantizar isso, não por que os criadores quiserem muito das vezes, mas por que é assim que a sétima arte se depõe em nossos olhos e signos. Dito isso, a obra de Edward Berger anda em um liminar tão amedrontador, com um visual tão profundo e melancólico, criticaram as esferas de mais privilégios as bases mais sofridas de uma guerra que por um momento parece que a súmula de Truffaut se equivoca aqui, mas tudo isso para demonstrar que às vezes a maior busca por um sentimento antiguerra traz o amor a guerra. O diretor resolve adicionar a essa obra de trilhagem tão interessante e obscura, com retoques de profundidade de símbolos inclusos como é o exemplo da raposa e das florestas, para no fim adaptar de certa forma uma espécie de jornada do herói. O começo do filme é didático em mostrar um dos melhores acertos do filme, a guerra aqui é trabalhada como produto, como venda. Os soldados morrendo, as costureiras refazendo uniformes, as substituições… tudo aqui mostra um tom legível de repetição e precificação da vida de cidadãos, atitudes essas que realmente acontecem em tempos de guerra. E quando o filme volta para essa leitura é quando ele mais acerta na minha opinião. Todavia, o filme ainda não se desprende totalmente de uma leitura protagonista, jornada e inclusive tem ate mentor. Esse ponto não necessariamente é ruim, tendo em vista que muitas vezes são esses laços que passam a mensagem de humanidade em um cenário de morte, porém é perceptível que na maioria dos filmes grandes de guerra, aqui não diferente, neste posso de sujeira, sangue e morte há um quê de realismo, sempre tem, “o meu filme de guerra tem mais tons de real e de verdade” e quando se tenta sair na contramão da citação que falei no começo deste texto é quando se dá conta do tom persuasivo e nada antiguerra de um filme. O protagonista aqui possui laços, possui dor e temos medo de perder os amigos dele, e isso é um romance de guerra no final das contas! é ruim? É bom? É o cinema persuadindo nós mais uma vez. __dantas

The Western Front during World War I. The back-and-forth war of attrition between the German and Allied forces is depicted from the perspective of the German army, as seen through a German lens. The fact that this is a German remake—rather than a remake of the 1930 Hollywood version—further emphasizes the futility and emptiness of war. This film received nine nominations at the 2023 Academy Awards. World War I, which lasted four years, radically transformed the technology and tactics of warfare. It featured aerial combat with strategic bombers, naval battles involving U-boats, and land battles in the trenches using tanks, flamethrowers, and chemical weapons. The film vividly and passionately depicts the ferocious land battles in which a combined total of 10 million soldiers from both sides lost their lives. Yet the people there are not heroes. Dressed in recycled combat uniforms still bearing bullet holes, they are sent to the front lines as reinforcements, just like bullets. Whether they are seasoned warriors or friends, there is no divine intervention regarding whether they will survive. It all comes down to whether or not they are hit by a bullet until the very moment the war ends. What does this imply for the subsequent World War II, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the conflicts that will likely continue to recur? This is the question posed by Germany.

I just watched All Quiet on the Western Front, and, okay, I didn't fully watch it. I actually DNFed it. I didn't finish it. And it's not because it's a bad movie. This movie won four Oscars, and I can't complain about the visuals, the acting, the screenplay, or really anything about how the movie was made. The only thing that made me DNF it is that I just couldn't get into it. I tried. I genuinely tried sticking through it, and I just couldn't. Here's the thing for me. I just wasn't able to develop any kind of connection to the characters. Paul, to me, just felt like another young man and another character. I can't remember for the life of me who the other four people are, whether they're his friends, his higher ups, or whatever. And because I couldn't develop that connection with any of them, it became really hard for me to root for them. I know that sounds horrible, but I just found myself not being able to get into it. I couldn't sit there for more than ten minutes without eventually looking around my room or getting distracted, and that's sort of a deal breaker for me when I'm watching a movie. I think a lot of people are probably going to be disappointed with my take on this. I'm sure some people would tell me that I don't know what I'm talking about or that I just don't understand the movie, but I genuinely tried to give it a chance. I mean, I made it about three fourths of the way through the movie before finally giving up. I just couldn't find myself rooting for Paul or really any of the other characters. Obviously, when they're in battle, I'm rooting for Paul and his buddies to survive and make it through, but there wasn't that deeper emotional connection where I genuinely felt attached to them. I think one of the reasons this movie still gets three stars from me is because it does an incredible job of showing the horrifying reality of trench warfare during World War I. And if I'm being so honest, I was really interested in seeing more of that side of the war. I'm not going to say I wanted to see trench foot, but trench foot was a massive part of the horrible conditions soldiers experienced during World War I, and I was interested in seeing more of those details. I'm glad I got to see the flamethrowers, the tanks, the actual trenches, and just how brutal and terrifying that kind of warfare was. Those parts were genuinely interesting to me. But even with all of that, I just couldn't get into the actual movie. I don't know what it is. Sometimes a movie just doesn't connect with you, and this one didn't connect with me. So I'll give All Quiet on the Western Front three stars out of five, and that's really only because I couldn't get into it. This movie isn't bad whatsoever. The visuals aren't bad. The acting isn't bad. The storyline isn't bad. The screenplay, the cinematography, the coloring, all of it is incredibly well done. I can completely understand why other people love this movie and why it won the awards that it did. It just wasn't for me. That's it.

Bleak as hell, but pretty damn effective. I really liked how completely this strips war of any grandeur and reduces it to mud, panic, exhaustion, and young men being fed into this enormous machine for objectives that become increasingly abstract and meaningless. It’s huge in scale without ever confusing scale for heroism, and I think that distinction is where the movie is strongest. The brutality lands because it rarely feels ornamental; it’s constantly reinforcing the idea that war functions through attrition, reducing individual lives to bodies, numbers, and territory gained or lost. I never connected with the characters quite enough for it to completely devastate me, but the human cost still registers, especially in the quieter moments where all the military rhetoric falls away and you’re just left with frightened people trying to survive. Really well made, appropriately miserable, and impressively committed to its anti-war perspective. It didn’t hit me on some profound emotional level, but I admired a lot of what it was doing, particularly how effectively it makes the entire machinery of war feel both enormous and completely fucking senseless.

Forging your parent's signature for a field trip is good.  Forging your parent's signature to join an ongoing war is bad. The 2022 adaptation of Erich Maria Remarque's seminal anti-war novel isn't what I'd call a remake of Lewis Milestone's Best Picture-winning film from 1930 (or the Delbert Mann version which was made for television in 1979) but rather another interpretation of the story.  It's the same sentiment I have regarding the new Sense and Sensibility coming out.  Rather than remaking the Ang Lee one, it appears to just be the next go-around of filming Jane Austen's book. Director Edward Berger goes all in on the "war is hell" imagery here.  His tasteful eye, combined with the astonishingly great cinematography by James Friend, allows All Quiet on the Western Front a certain visceral heft that may not have been possible given the constraints of its earlier predecessors.  Nothing in the film is particularly new if you've seen its contemporaries but it still manages to achieve its purpose emotionally, thematically and cinematically. Just to get my negative out of the way, I don't get why Volker Bertelmann snagged the Oscar here.  Those three notes sound too much like dubstep for my taste.  Anachronistic scores can work but it took me out.  That said, Bertelmann's other compositions in the film are quite effective but maybe I'm bitter that Justin Hurwitz's Babylon score, easily one of the decade's most memorable film soundtracks, lost to this.  Then again, considering the same branch didn't even nominate Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross for Challengers, I can't say I'm surprised. Felix Kammerer gives a remarkable debut performance.  His face screams someone whose pure innocence will be decimated by the brutality of war, not unlike the young boy from Come and See.  Albrecht Schuch is great too as Kat.  He was a highlight from that Berlin Alexanderplatz in 2020.  Daniel Brühl is easily the most recognizable actor here, lending credibility as Matthias Erzberger, a German politician instrumental in the armistice that ended the war. I was mesmerized by Berger's command of the camera.  He puts you down and dirty in those trenches.  It's a harmonious mixture of some phenomenal production design by Christian M. Goldbeck, seamless integration of visual effects and some awesome makeup that cakes our actors in mud to resemble the horrifically obscuring conditions that it takes to engage in this level of combat.  There's a reason Paul goes from smiling and chipper at the start to absolutely stone-faced by the end. The assembly line nature of the youth as they enter their regiments is frightening.  A batch of young soldiers dies only to be replaced by younger soldiers whose eyes can't fathom the terrifying things they're about to inflict and be inflicted upon.  The scene of Paul engaging in a one-on-one with the French soldier is devastating because it's a fight or flight scenario while also an acknowledgement of how war encourages the loss of our humanity little by little until we can't even comprehend the actions we commit. Paul is one of many millions of people who were indoctrinated into thinking that what they were doing was a good thing and that the future tales of heroics will far exceed anything on the battlefield.  Meanwhile, the people with the power to the end the war only did so when it mathematically didn't make sense to continue and even still there were those who pridefully refused to concede, thus dragging on the war.  You just become numb to it all, senseless to the feeling that you're a pawn, an eventual casualty in a long list of obituaries. If the Germans pulled a Reynolds Woodcock and simply sewed the names into the fabric it'd make the whole recycling uniforms thing easier.

All Quiet on the Western Front is one of a small group of Netflix original movies that is both impressive to look at and actually worth watching. Sure it isn’t a particularly unique story, instead essentially playing as a remake of a remake, but if you’re looking for a brutal and striking depiction of war then you’ll be hard pressed to find better. What fascinates me about war is that despite every distinct conflict being inherently awful, each of them are terrible in their own unique way. You’ve obviously got the raw numbers with WW2, the insanity and trauma of Vietnam and the boredom of the Gulf war, but I honestly don’t think anything can ever top WW1. It’s kinda the perfect culmination of everything awful people associate about war. It happened at a time when people still thought fighting and dying for your country was honourable, so you had poor recruits thinking they were going on an adventure and generals who thought any problem could just be solved by throwing bodies at them. You’ve also got undoubtedly some of the worst conditions in any modern conflict with the trenches and their mud, disease and rats, on top of the insanity element thanks to spending years fighting for a few extra metres and watching your friends get blown to pieces. Truly as far as picking a bad experience to live through, I think you’d be hard pressed to find anything worse than ‘The Great War’ and All Quiet on the Western Front really excellently captures that vibe. What this movies really excels at is getting across how every soldier as an individual was treated like absolute dirt. They were given hammy down clothes from the last lot who had been slaughtered and then sent to die in the mud just so some stuck up boffins could pat themselves on the back and eat a fancy pastry. Their lives were viewed as completely without value besides dying for their country, despite each of them being people in their own right with families and hopes. The fact that this story is told from a distinctly German perspective further helps manifest that idea, since ultimately every young man in every country during the war got the same speech about how righteous they were and how they will bring glory to their fatherland. They couldn’t all be right and realistically none of them were. It’s easy to solidify yourself in the ‘us vs them’ mindset when looking at historical conflicts, hence why stories like this one are so important. That scene in the mortar crater really gets the point across. Everyone was told to hate and kill each other, but looking in the eyes of another innocent young lad and taking his life away remains genuinely one of the most horrific things you could be forced to do. Scenes like that are used effectively throughout All Quiet on the Western Front and really draw into question the inhumanity that was rife during WW1. The other aspect of All Quiet which is undoubtedly great is how terrific it looks. Maybe it’s because I’m used to the green screen/volume vibe of most straight to Netflix movies, but this movie really blew me away from the visuals. The cinematography is gorgeous with its use of colours and its framing of the central events, sometimes heightening the tension like with that tank sequence and sometimes contrasting the chaos with more quiet, tender moments. I wasn’t expecting this movie to be as Terrence Malick as it is, but it’s quite a nice homage to movies like The Thin Red Line whilst further helping demonstrate the shear chaos unleashed by the war. On that note, the gore in this movie is also excellent. It doesn’t pull any punches, with bodies just lying everywhere, often missing parts, all whilst being framed with such a blasé and unfazed perspective. It’s an essential aspect of capturing the vibe of this conflict, given that soldiers at the time had to live around decaying corpses rife with disease all whilst never knowing if they or their mates would be next. All Quiet honestly gets pretty dark at times and I really appreciate it. It’s absolutely not afraid to delve into the traumatic and damaged mindset of the German soldiers, making the movie overall all the more effective. All that glazing being said, I had heard claims that this was an easy contender for ‘the best war movie ever made’ and I just don’t know if I’d agree. It’s very good don’t get me wrong, but it feels like it’s missing something that the best of the genre absolutely aren’t. I can’t help but get the feeling that the ending of this movie and the emotional stakes would have been much more impactful if the first half an hour wasn’t so rushed. I haven’t seen the original in completion, but I understand that a big part is dedicated to introducing the characters and seeing them be all excited and giddy before they go off to war. In this version, it kinda feels like the filmmakers were anxious to get them straight into conflict and as a result only left maybe three scenes of the characters before they become damaged (maybe the Netflix influence creeped in there). Whilst I do think that their descent into nihilism is portrayed effectively, I would have liked to get to know the characters a bit more before they became broken. Some war movies can get away with having bland characters because they frame their stories as something that could have just happened to anyone, but All Quiet definitely feels like it’s trying to zoom in and tell a personal story and I’m not sure it’s done as well as people say. I couldn’t really name any of the characters other than Paul, and even then I can’t say I related to him personally, outside of his situation which everyone else around him was also in. I feel like if I really liked him and his mates as guys, then that ending scene would have been brutal, but as is I was almost indifferent. Their fates were quite predictable and at the end of the day they were all probably better off than if they were forced to continue their suffering. Something like Saving Private Ryan for example always leaves me shattered since I love those characters so much, but the same doesn’t really apply to All Quiet. Maybe another little thing, and this is more of a personal problem than an objective complaint, but the scope of the story just didn’t particularly strike me. All Quiet kinda feels like it’s running the gamut of WW1 things, and whilst they’re all done very well individually, the way they are all connected together to produce the final narrative felt a little lacking. It’s just Paul running from battle to battle trying to survive without any particular goal in mind. It’s a tough complaint for sure, but in such an overplayed genre where every major conflict has been covered by a dozen famous movies (in this case also the exact same story multiple times)  I think All Quiet feels a little bit lacking in what it has to offer. Even if the ideas are very strong, they have absolutely been covered elsewhere and have been occasionally done just as well, which in my eyes makes this movie feel a tad more generic than it probably should. A very good watch all and all. It’s probably one of the few foreign language films that you could convince your dad to watch and there is absolutely a reason for it. Even if it isn’t the most original or character driven story, it would be pretty hard to execute this narrative much better. Maybe that means we won’t get a fourth go at it, but with how creatively bankrupt executives are nowadays I honestly wouldn’t be surprised. Watch this space.

In my line of work, we often omit the usage of the word “remains” — if nothing has changed, it should be left unsaid. But “remains” can mean a lot of things. What hasn’t changed, the splintering of bodies, what is left behind. The main audial motif of the movie is titled “remains”, and the audience is almost berated with it, like the relentless barrage of artillery fire, again and again and again and again. Its scenes feel almost post-apocalyptic in its delivery of the past. What was once memory is now history. History tends to mysteriously vanish, a case of the universal forgetting. The lessons learnt are what remains. But nothing remains at all except remains. Even that is buried on unmarked soil. And to think that, after humanity has gone through so much in a little over a century, it has learnt nothing. Perhaps nothing has really changed, and that is the most upsetting of all.
